examples.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Matrix Polynomial Using the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem
examples.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & -5 \\ 3 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\  & =(4-\lambda )(-4-\lambda )+15 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:

|  | $\:\:x^{10}$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x^2-1\:$ | $\!\require{enclose}\enclose{longdiv}{x^{12} \, - \, x^{10}  +  2x  -  1 {\phantom{|}} }$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  | $x^{12}$ | $-$ | $x^{10}$ |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  |  |  | $2x$ | $-$ | $1$ |

Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\  & ={x}^{10}({x}^{2}-1)+(2x-1),\end{aligned}
$$

where $q(x) = x^{10}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have

$$
f(A) = q(A)p(A)+(2A-I).
$$

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(2A-I) \\  & =q(A)\cdot O+(2A-I) \\  & =2A-I \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}4 & -5 \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -10 \\ 6 & -8\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -10 \\ 6 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & -3-\lambda  & 0 \\ 7 & -5 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 \\ -1 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )((2-\lambda )(-3-\lambda )+1) & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -5) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}+2{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda -5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{3}+2{A}^{2}-4A-5I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{3}+2{A}^{2}-4A-5I) & =O \\ {A}^{2}+2A-4I-5{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =-\frac{4}{5}I+\frac{2}{5}A+\frac{1}{5}{A}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$
